St-Pierre J.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Ottawa (Ottawa, Ontario, Canada)
St-Pierre J.role: Biochemist and Vice-President, Research and Innovation at the University of Ottawa who studies how cancer cells adapt their metabolism, and a co-author on McGill work linking mTORC1 to mitochondria and to rapamycin-induced fatty liver
St-Pierre J.sub: Vice-President, Research and Innovation, University of Ottawa (interim appointment from October 2024) · Full professor, Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology, University of Ottawa (2017–) · Associate Vice-President, Research Support and Infrastructure, University of Ottawa (2023–2024) · Assistant professor to full professor, McGill University (2008–2017) · PhD, University of Cambridge
story: Julie St-Pierre is a co-author on two Atlas studies from McGill University about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and energy metabolism. The 2013 Cell Metabolism paper (MOR2013), led by Nahum Sonenberg's group, showed in cells that mTORC1 sets how many mitochondria a cell builds and how hard they work. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations. mTORC1 does this by releasing the brake that 4E-BP proteins put on the production of proteins the mitochondria need. This links the growth signal directly to the energy supply that growth needs.

The 2026 Journal of Endocrinology paper (BCH2026), from Vincent Giguère's group, is a mouse study. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, can cause fatty liver, and adding the antimalarial drug chloroquine made that fatty liver milder. The rescue depended on ERR-alpha, a nuclear receptor that switches on many energy metabolism genes; in mice without it, chloroquine did not help.

St-Pierre studied at Laval University in Quebec (BSc and MSc), earned a doctorate at the University of Cambridge in England, and did postdoctoral research in Europe and the United States, including at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. From 2008 to 2017 St-Pierre was on the faculty of McGill University, rising from assistant to full professor, and co-founded and co-led a metabolomics core facility there for eight years. Metabolomics measures hundreds of small molecules of metabolism at once and gives a snapshot of a cell's metabolic state. In 2018 St-Pierre was also a co-author on the McGill study of how ERR-alpha shapes fatty liver on a high-fat diet. The main research theme is how breast cancer cells change their metabolism, and how those changes can help tumours resist treatment.

In 2017 the University of Ottawa recruited St-Pierre to set up a similar metabolomics facility in its Faculty of Medicine, with a professorship in the Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology. St-Pierre became the university's Associate Vice-President, Research Support and Infrastructure in 2023, and took over as Vice-President, Research and Innovation in October 2024, first on an interim basis. The 2026 paper lists St-Pierre at both the Goodman Cancer Institute in Montreal and the University of Ottawa.

Deleu I.role: Medical oncologist in Sint-Niklaas, Belgium, who enrolled patients in international breast cancer drug trials, including the BOLERO-2 trial of everolimus
Deleu I.sub: Medical oncologist, oncology department, Vitaz hospital, Sint-Niklaas (named in a 2024 news report) · Oncologic Centre, AZ Nikolaas, Sint-Niklaas (PubMed affiliation 2011–2022)
story: Ines Deleu is a co-author of the two Atlas reports from BOLERO-2, a large trial in postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer that is driven by hormones (hormone-receptor-positive) and does not carry extra copies of the HER2 gene. These cancers often learn to grow despite hormone treatment, and switching on the mTOR pathway is one way they do it. BOLERO-2 added everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to the hormone drug exemestane. The first report (BAS2012) showed that the combination kept the cancer from growing for several months longer than exemestane alone. The final report (PIC2014) found that this gain held up, but that overall survival was not significantly longer (31.0 against 26.6 months).

Large cancer trials like this one run at hundreds of hospitals, and site investigators enrol and treat the patients, collect the data and sign off on the final paper. PubMed lists Deleu at AZ Nikolaas, a general hospital in Sint-Niklaas in Flanders, on about a dozen papers, most of them multicentre breast cancer trials. The most recent, from 2022, is the phase III EMERALD trial of elacestrant, an oral drug that breaks down the estrogen receptor.

A 2024 news report on public tours of the oncology department at Vitaz hospital in Sint-Niklaas names Dr. Ines Deleu as the oncologist who leads them, explaining cancer statistics and treatment options to visitors and pointing out a room set up for adolescents and young adults with cancer. No official hospital profile was found, so training details are not given here.
